entry.title: New Rewritable Antimony Elenide Display Shows an Image for Months Without Power
entry.content:
New Rewritable Displays Can Show an Image For Months Without Power 24 Nov, 2026

Researchers from the ARC Centre of Excellence for Transformative Meta-Optical Systems (TMOS) are the first to report a reflective display based on Antimony Selenide that can hold an image for months without being powered.

Everyday displays, such as the ones found in your phone, laptop, or television, require a constant power draw to maintain an image. However, now, reflective displays are emerging as a sustainable alternative that could offer near zero power consumption while maintaining an image.

In a cross-node collaboration at TMOS, researchers from the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) and the Australian National University (ANU) have demonstrated the promise of Antimony Selenide (Sb2Se3) a material for lower-power displays by building and testing a reflective platform capable of retaining an image for months without power, being reliably reusable, and offering a wide colour gamut.

The lead researcher, Dr Phuong Yen Le, says, âThis is a new way to create energy-efficient displays.â

Their study was published in Advanced Photonics Research.

The Technology

The key to the new display technology is an unusual type of material that Dr Le has been excited to study for a long time: phase change materials (PCMs).

Unlike most materials, PCMs can be rearranged repeatedly at the atomic level by selectively applying stimuli, such as heat, light, or electricity.

These stimuli can be used to rearrange the structure of the atoms, or âphaseâ, of the material from amorphous (irregular arrangements of atoms) to crystalline (highly ordered arrangements of atoms) and back again.

It is this capacity to be reordered that has interested Dr Le for a long time.

âI think phase change materials are really, really cool [â¦] Most materials always stay in one structure, so if you choose crystallised arrangement during fabrication [â¦] any application is going to be fixed to that material structure. But these [PCMs] can change so you get different optical and electrical properties.â

What makes Antimony Selenide desirable among PCMs is its non-volatility. Once it changes phase, it is locked and does not require continuous power to maintain its state.

Creating Colour

This is a promising tool, but to make a display, Dr Le and the research teams first needed to understand how best to produce a range of colours and shades with PCMs.

One of the reasons for choosing Antimony Selenide how significantly its interaction with light changed between the crystalline and amorphous forms.

Light travelling through the different phases moves at different speeds and is absorbed to different degrees. It was these effects that could be leveraged to produce different colours.

From Dr Leâs perspective, understanding the relationship between phase and colour was the main thrust of the research.

âThis work is really about characterising Antimony Selenide. We wanted to understand how changes in its structure affect its optical properties and how those optical changes can be used to create different colours in a device.â

Combining the investigation of phase with different thicknesses of the Antimony Selenide, the researchers produced colours ranging from deep blues through to greys and oranges.

But Dr Le says this is just the start of the colour possibilities.

âAt the moment, this structure only gives us a limited range of colours. The next step is to understand what changes to the deviceâs structure will make more colours accessible and expand the colour gamut.â

Drawing and Erasing

So, how is this material rearranged at the atomic level to produce these colours? It is a little like trying to change glass into quartz and back again repeatedly.

The answer: heat and lasers!

Erasing the display was done by heating the material to ~200Â°C uniformly; at this temperature, the atoms have enough energy to move around and find new positions and orientations.

At these high temperatures, atoms can migrate into the most stable positions, which tend to be crystals due to the dense packing of their regular structure.

This process is known as annealing, and it resets the display with a uniform blank image.

Then, to draw images on the blank screen, co-author Dr Shvedov used short laser pulses, like drawing with a laser instead of a pencil.

The laser pulses add just enough energy to get the atoms moving again and into irregular arrangements, but crucially, this is done quickly.

As the regions hit with the laser cool down quickly, the atoms freeze in their new irregular arrangement before without a chance to settle back into their crystalline configuration.

This leaves them fixed in their amorphous phase, resulting in different coloured regions.

The Results

Putting it all to the test, a variety of images, including a map of Australia, the TMOS logo, and a koala, were drawn and erased on the display.

The researchers found that there was no residual image after annealing, even when inspected under a 5Ã magnification microscope.

But even more surprisingly, the image of a koala was imprinted on the material and left for three months under ambient conditions without any noticeable change.

And in fact, Dr Le tells us it has lasted even longer.

âActually, I still have that image with me. It still looks the same a year later.â

These were promising results for developing this display technology further, and Dr Le already had some avenues to cover to get to true commercial energy-efficient displays.

âRight now, it uses a laser. It needs to be a fully electrical device as well. So currently Iâm working on testing the electrical characteristics of the material [â¦] and if we want to have more colour, we may need to change the structure.â

Nonvolatile, Rewritable, Multilevel Reflective Displays Based on Antimony Selenide Thin Films

Phuong Y. Le, Vladlen Shvedov, Yana Izdebskaya, Peter F. M. Elango, Krishna Murali, Ilya V. Shadrivov, Sharath Sriram, Madhu Bhaskaran

Advanced Photonics Research, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1002/adpr.70305

Abstract:

Reflective display technologies are emerging as a sustainable alternative to traditional emissive systems, offering the potential for near-zero static power consumption. Chalcogenide phase change materials, with their nonvolatile nature and reversible structural transformations between their phases, represent promising candidates for such applications. Here, we demonstrate a multilevel, rewritable display platform based on a thin film of the phase-change material antimony selenide (Sb2Se3). By integrating Sb2Se3 into a multilayer interference stack, the resonant optical response can be precisely modulated through thickness engineering and active control of the materialâs crystallinity. We demonstrate that nanosecond laser pulses can induce multiple intermediate states, expanding the accessible color gamut beyond binary switching. The devices exhibit excellent rewritability and long-term stability, with images persisting for months without degradation. These findings position Sb2Se3 as a promising candidate for next-generation, nonvolatile displays and high-density optical information storage.

entry.title: The Artificial Monkey Mind
entry.content:
I’ve been practising meditation for decades, but I’m barely a beginner. What I find most challenging is what the Buddhists call the monkey mind. Instead of being aware of the moment, my brain is elsewhere. It’s dwelling on the past or worrying about the future, rather than paying attention to what’s happening right now.

It is not possible to stop this kind of thinking. That’s just what brains do. The goal is to let my thoughts go and not get caught up in them. I practise regularly to learn how to remain detached from that chaotic stream, to just observe it and not follow or react. I want to be able to make conscious choices about where I spend my attention.

Maybe someday I’ll manage whole seconds of this ideal state.

It occurred to me recently that we are now dealing with a kind of artificial monkey mind in large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT or Claude. They mimic our own thinking so well that we anthropomorphise them. They appeal to our monkey minds in a way no previous technology has. I’m talking daily with people who seem to be verging on an unhealthy connection to these things, using them like a therapist or a GP, for example. They’re getting caught up in the chatbot’s responses, just as we get caught up in our thoughts.

But despite the technical twist, this isn’t a new problem. People have been trying to tame the mental chatter and instinct-driven behaviour for thousands of years. From ancient Hindu and Buddhist traditions, through early Christian and Islamic contemplation, to modern mindfulness, humans have been struggling to rise above the clattering cacophony since at least the beginning of civilisation.

LLMs are a uniquely powerful distraction, but I wonder if these practices could teach us to interact with them in a healthier way.

The thinking mind

The part of the mind that “thinks” is the “doing” part of our brain. It’s a what-if engine or analyser, taking often fragmentary and incomplete evidence from our senses and building a theory of reality in real time. By necessity, the mind fills in the gaps in its data. It confabulates. It’s not hallucinating, exactly – we’re not hearing voices – but we are unknowingly making up facts to fit our current picture of the world.

The brain also has basic assumptions, many of which are wrong. My impostor syndrome, which I’ve written about before, is one example of that kind of distortion. There’s also depression or other forms of mental illness.

But the tendency to misread reality is more basic than that and affects everyone. Our instincts come into play. For example, getting along with others in the tribe, troop or herd has kept us alive for millions of years, so it’s a powerful urge.

With our eagerness to find patterns and our subconscious instincts, it’s no wonder that we have a hard time staying in the moment.

With chatbots, it’s even worse. We dealing with two monkey minds that play off each other. We assume we understand what the LLM – that statistically generated, stochastic parrot – is on about (pattern matching), agree with it and just become its yes man. Our instinct to gel, to go with the flow, is also triggered. An LLM doesn’t just sound like another person. It sounds like one who’s eager to agree with us. Flattery goes a long way!

Learning detachment

The counterpart to the thinking mind’s “doing” mode is our “being” mode. This is our awareness, our consciousness, or what some call the soul. It’s where we experience reality. Meditation in all its forms aims to help us get to a state where we are fully aware of the present moment (the only moment we have, really) and where we are fully free to experience it, just as it is, with as few distortions as possible.

Detaching from our monkey mind, with its bad assumptions and distortions, is part of developing wisdom. At its most basic, wisdom is a sceptical attitude toward your own thinking. The wise one has learnt that they are often wrong, that first impressions are often misleading, that the best-laid plans go awry. The wise aren’t attached to their own attitudes or theories. They readily adjust when facts don’t fit any longer.

The daily practice of meditation is like exercising the mental muscles we need to walk this path. We gently bring our attention back, without judging ourselves for drifting. In mindfulness, for example, we connect with reality in a simple, physical way: focusing our attention on the sensation of breathing. The key skill is to notice when we’ve been carried away from the present moment. It’s this, in particular, that I think will help us most with LLMs.

So, when our minds or an LLM deliver a verdict with confidence, we should say “That’s nice” or “Good boy” and treat it as another hypothesis to test. Instead, we fail to notice that we’re being carried away by this stream. We stop paying attention.

No daydreaming

Of course, as my decades of flailing with meditation have taught me, it’s a lot easier said than done. As a general rule, we’re pretty helpless in the face of the egotistical monkey mind. It’s our mind, after all, and we’re pretty attached to it. We give it the benefit of the doubt, completely unconsciously. And LLMs do a pretty good job now, and are getting better, at ingratiating themselves with us.

When using an LLM, it’s really tricky to remain engaged – to bring ourselves, fully and attentively, to what we’re doing. It’s very easy to get lulled into the flow with an LLM – just like it’s easy to daydream.

I mostly use LLMs for programming, so what works for me might not work for people who use them for other kinds of work. The aim is to stay present and grounded. One trick I use is to make my LLMs speak “caveman” – simple, no unnecessary words, no fluff. Just the facts. I’m less likely to treat them like people or to get stupefied by a wall of words.

Another method is to use the LLM to plan, but do the work myself. I took a similar approach with Stack Overflow. I’d search for an answer, but I wouldn’t paste it into my code. I’d type it out, line by line. Just doing that engages your attention surprisingly well. I find myself making small changes, more fitting to my style, taste and the actual specifics of the problem at hand, even if I’m just copying someone else’s work or following another’s plan.

Finally, and most importantly, I limit my use of these things. Do I need to use an LLM for this? If I’m so lost in the code that I can’t work out where to make a small change, something’s wrong. I’m no longer in charge.

Magic

When I first started using LLMs for coding at work – mostly for auto-completion – they were quite clunky and stupid. But modern models are getting good. They almost feel miraculous. On code I’m especially familiar with, I can use LLMs to offload a lot of drudgery. When I know the architecture and the trade-offs that have been made, I can set the guardrails correctly and ask for specific things to be done – and the work gets done, like magic, much faster than I could do it by hand.

But over time, if I continuously use LLMs to do everything, the code becomes less and less familiar. I start losing touch.

Now that I’m retiring, I’m wondering if it makes sense to use LLMs at all. At work, when I need to upgrade the runtimes of a dozen AWS Lambda functions by a particular deadline, I can justify using LLMs to churn through those kinds of tedious tasks much faster and more efficiently. But at home, I don’t have those kinds of time pressures. I’m doing the work because I’m having fun learning something new. I learn best by doing, by trial and error.

What am I using LLMs for, exactly?

entry.title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
entry.content:
LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you

5 min read

In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?

Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.

So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.

It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks

Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.

So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone???

This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!

Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra.

Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget.

And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now.

This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for me and have my best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example.

On the existential threat or tool question, I'm firmly in the tool camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions.

And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this. ↩︎

entry.title: Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on one port
entry.content:
Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on One Port

November 23, 2026

I started building restorekit.org dongles a few months ago at the Recurse Center. They are small inline USB-C boards that sit between a host computer and a target mac. They set the target mac into DFUDevice Firmware Update: Apple's lowest-level recovery mode built into the boot ROM, so even a bricked Mac can be reflashed. mode over USB-PDUSB Power Delivery: the communication protocol over the CC wire used to negotiate power, roles, and vendor-defined commands. without having to touch the target at all, and work with an open-source toolkit for restoring macs without the need for another mac.

The original board, the Dongle-Lite, is USB 2 only. A single USB 2 hub (CH334F) connects both the dongle’s MCU and the target mac through a single cable, while a PD PHYPhysical-layer transceiver chip that encodes and decodes USB Power Delivery packets on the CC wire. (FUSB302B) sends Apple’s DFU commands on the CC line.

I recently learned from timo at Twocanoes that newer Macs support USB 3 speeds for recovery. I obviously immediately wanted to support this on the hub for faster recovery, but the problem was cost. At first I designed a “proper” USB 3 board using a GL3510 USB 3 hub and a pair of TI SuperSpeed muxes (HD3SS3220 and HD3SS3212). It basically doubled the parts count, and BOMBill of Materials: the full list of components and quantities required to assemble one board. cost, required me to increase the size of PCB to ~100 mm, and topped out at 5 Gbps transfers between host and target (USB 3.1 Gen 1).

I really didn’t want to make a board that cost more than twice the Dongle-Lite just to get USB 3 speeds.

So with the 2nd version Dongle-Pro, I tried a kinda crazy USB-C experiment: drop the USB 3 hub completely, keep a cheap USB 2 hub on D+/D-, and route the USB 3 SuperSpeedUSB 3.x's dedicated high-speed TX/RX differential pairs, physically separate from USB 2's D+/D- wires. lanes as a straight passthrough from host to target on the same USB-C port. The idea being that in theory the USB 3 and 2 controllers on a USB-C are completely independent, and should work simultaneously.

Since high-speed USB 3 is super prone to interference I didn’t really have a choice other than to purchase a view boards and test it out.

Well… I just got the boards in from JLC and… THEY WORK! They establish a full 10 Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 connection while connecting the dongle’s USB 2 hub and MCU over the exact same port. After some aggressive cost optimization, the 10 Gbps board also ended up cheaper and smaller than the USB 2 Dongle-Lite.

How USB 3 and USB 2 Share a Port

Like I mentioned earlier, USB-C is not a single data bus. Inside a standard USB-C port, USB 2 and USB 3 sit on completely different sets of pins:

Every USB-C port has two mirrored 12-pin rows: A1 through A12 on top, and B12 through B1 on the bottom, so a cable works rotated either way.

USB 2 (D+ / D-): a single 480 Mbps pair in the center (pins A6/A7 and B6/B7 are shorted together). USB 3 (TX/RX): 2 separate high-speed lanes on the outer edge. Only 1 set is active depending on orientation. Control & sideband (CC, SBU): CC1/CC2 detect cable orientation and negotiate USB-PD; SBU1/SBU2 (A8/B8) are used by Apple’s 1.2 V debug UART.

This continues to the computer’s xHCIExtensible Host Controller Interface: the USB controller inside your computer that manages both USB 2 and USB 3.x root ports. controller: a single physical USB-C port is actually wired to two independent root ports: a USB 2 port and a USB 3 port.

A standard USB 3 hub chip like the GL3510 is actually just two hubs in 1 package (a USB 2 hub and a USB 3 hub). On my first iteration of the Dongle-Pro, everything ran through that chip even though the dongle’s own MCU only speaks USB 2 Full Speed (12 Mbps) and has no need for the USB 3 speed.

On the Dongle-Pro v2, the two buses are split apart:

USB 2 (D+/D-) runs into a CH334P USB 2 hub. One downstream port goes to the target’s D+/D- (so DFU mode and any USB 2 device behave just like the Lite), and another goes to the dongle’s MCU (CH32X035G8U6). USB 3 (TX/RX) skips the hub completely. Each port’s two lane sets go into a CH9441P 2:1 muxMultiplexer: a high-speed analog switch that routes whichever side of a reversible USB-C plug is active onto one pair of board traces.. Each mux reads its own port’s CC1/CC2 lines to handle cable flip and connects the active lane set to its common side. The two muxes sit in the center of the board, wired straight together through a short corridor with no hub and no redriverAn active signal-conditioning chip that boosts and equalizes high-speed USB 3 traces to overcome cable and PCB insertion loss.. What Could Go Wrong

This sounded like it would work to me on paper, but there were a few things I thought could go wrong:

Two passive muxes in series with no redriver. Every connector, ESD array, via, and switch adds insertion loss and reflections. I was hoping two CH9441P chips back-to-back would pass 5 Gbps. But hitting 10 Gbps is even better. Sharing the target CC lines. On the target port, the HUSB311 PD PHY actively drives the CC lines to send Apple’s SOP” DebugA USB-PD packet framing addressed to a debug accessory rather than a normal device, required for Apple's DFU commands. VDMsVendor-Defined Messages: custom USB-PD packets. Apple uses them to trigger DFU, reboot, and serial debug without touching the keyboard.. The target’s CH9441P is also reading the lines to steer its lanes. Host OS behavior. Even though it made sense in theory, I really wasn’t sure if a machine would happily enumerate a USB 2 hub on a port’s D+/D- lines while a separate USB 3.2 Gen 2 device negotiated directly with the same port’s SuperSpeed lanes. On the Bench

When the boards arrived, I immediately plugged one into my mac, plugged an iPhone into the target port, and inspected the bus with system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType and ioreg -p IOUSB.

Here is what macOS sees on a single physical USB-C port (AppleT8132USBXHCI@01000000):

The raw system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType output shows both sides active at once:

0x01100000 is the USB 2 half of the physical port, and 0x01200000 is the SuperSpeed half of the same port. The iPhone enumerated straight through both passive CH9441P muxes at 10 Gb/s (USB 3.2 Gen 2), while the CH334P hub and Dongle-Pro-v2 MCU enumerate at 480 Mb/s and 12 Mb/s on D+/D-.

Companion Ports

Splitting the bus required one interesting change in the host SDK (restorekit).

On the Dongle-Lite, whatever device you plugged into the dongle always showed up as a child of the dongle’s hub. That made it easy to tell which target Mac belonged to which dongle when you plugged in several at once.

On the Dongle-Pro v2, that breaks whenever the target connects at USB 3. Just like iPhone@01200000 above, a SuperSpeed target bypasses the CH334P hub completely and shows up as a sibling directly on the host’s root hub.

Turns out the OS already tracks which USB 2 and USB 3 root ports share the same physical port and it exposes it directly:

On macOS, the USB 2 port’s IORegistrymacOS's live kernel tree of hardware devices, ports, and drivers, which you can inspect with ioreg. entry has a UsbProtocolCompanion (3.x) property containing the path to its SuperSpeed twin. On Linux, the USB 2 port’s sysfsLinux's virtual filesystem at /sys that exposes kernel devices, USB hubs, and physical port peer links. directory has a port/peer symlink pointing straight to the SuperSpeed port.

So restorekit can still know with 100% certainty which 10 Gbps device is plugged into which dongle.

Cutting the Cost

I originally planned to have a Dongle-Lite and significantly more expensive USB 3 Pro, but that means having to maintain two hardware lines, so if I could cut the cost of the USB 3 version to be comparably priced to the original Dongle-Lite it felt like a no brainer.

After I removed the GL3510 USB 3 hub from the original design, I went through the rest of the board to see what else I could cut:

SuperSpeed path: HD3SS3220 ($1.66) + HD3SS3212 ($1.55) + GL3510 ($1.23) came to $4.44 on Pro v1 for 5 Gbps. Two CH9441P muxes cost $0.47 total ($0.24 each) on Pro v2 for 10 Gbps. Pro v1’s SuperSpeed chips alone cost more than the entire Pro v2 BOM. MCU: Swapped the RP2354A + 3.3 uH inductor + crystal ($1.62) with a CH32X035G8U6 ($0.42), running off its internal 48 MHz HSIHigh-Speed Internal oscillator: an on-chip clock source that lets an MCU run without an external quartz crystal. with no crystal, no external inductor, and a built-in ROM USB bootloader. PD PHY: Swapped the FUSB302BMPX ($0.68) with a HUSB311BLA ($0.51). USB 2 hub: Swapped the CH334F ($0.53) with a CH334P ($0.31), which integrates the crystal load capacitors and drops two more passives. 1.2 V SBU UART level shifters: two 74AVC1T45 translators plus a dedicated TLV70212 1.2 V LDO ($0.79) became two HL2302 MOSFETs and a few resistors ($0.05) wired as common-gate level shifters. Unified ESD and passive discipline: swapped mixed USBLC6 + TPD4E05U06 parts for six H5VU25U flow-through arrays (JLCPCB Preferred Extended = $0 feeder fee), and limited the whole board to just three resistor values and three capacitor values.

Running the three BOMs against JLCPCB pricing:

Metric Dongle-Lite (USB 2) Dongle-Pro v1 (5 Gbps) Dongle-Pro v2 (10 Gbps) Board size 22.1 x 77.1 mm (17.0 cm²) 26.0 x 98.0 mm (25.5 cm²) 21.0 x 48.0 mm (10.1 cm²) Unique BOM lines 24 (11 Extended) 31 (15 Extended) 18 (8 Extended) Total placements 56 99 52 JLCPCB feeder fees $33 $45 $24 Parts / board @ qty 15 $5.03 ($7.23 w/ fees) $10.44 ($13.44 w/ fees) $2.93 ($4.53 w/ fees) Parts / board @ qty 100 $4.06 ($4.39 w/ fees) $8.24 ($8.69 w/ fees) $2.31 ($2.55 w/ fees)

(Parts and Extended feeder fees from JLCPCB’s catalog, excluding PCB fab and placement fees. V2 wins on fab cost too since it is 40% smaller than the Lite and 60% smaller than Pro v1, packing three boards into one 81 x 48 mm panel.)

These swaps resulted in a 72% BOM reduction from original Dongle-Pro while doubling the SuperSpeed link rate from 5 Gbps to 10 Gbps, and a 42% BOM reduction compared to the Dongle-Lite.

Conclusion

If you are building an inline USB-C tool where your MCU only needs a slow control channel and the host just needs fast passthrough to the downstream device, you might not need a USB 3 hub. USB-C gives you two independent buses in the same port.

Next up: A flash drive with USB 3.2 Gen 2 + 2 speeds?

entry.title: A training engine for your local model, using your idle compute
entry.content:
Install • How it works • Commands • Roadmap • Discord • Website

Use your local model as usual through opencode, pi or any OpenAI-compatible tool. While you work, Songe notices what happens after each of the model's actions: the tool result, the error, your next message. When your agent is quiet, it teaches the model to see those coming. A new version is used only if it passes its checks, and nothing ever leaves your machine.

Learns from how you work. Your corrections, stated preferences and the tools' errors become lessons for your own model. Two kinds of Dreams. A Quick Dream adds your preferences to the model's instructions in minutes; a Deep Dream trains the model itself while you are away. Safe by default. A new version is used only if it does better on your own conversations; one click goes back to any earlier version. Stays out of the way. Runs only when your agent is quiet, memory is free and the battery is fine, and stops the moment you are back. Private. No account, no telemetry, no cloud. Songe never runs your tools.

With uv or pipx (Python 3.11 or later):

uv tool install songe # or: pipx install songe songe init

No uv or pipx yet? Either installs in one line:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh # uv (or: brew install uv) brew install pipx # pipx on macOS (Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt install pipx)

Both give Songe its own environment in a lasting place, which its background service needs.

macOS with Homebrew:

brew tap sous-labs/tap brew trust sous-labs/tap # newer Homebrew asks this once brew install songe songe init

songe init finds your model server and your agents, shows what it will change, and asks once:

$ songe init Models 3 from LM Studio, listed under Songe Agent opencode → Songe models · default granite-4.2-3b-MLX-4bit Agent pi → Songe models · choose one with /model Data ~/Library/Application Support/songe Service starts at login Learning new conversations · starts when idle Replace loaded copy when a better version is ready Install? (Y/n)

Then pick a Songe model in your agent (opencode lists them as songe/songe/<name>), and work as usual.

Plain pip, and what you need

pip install songe works inside a virtual environment; outside one, Homebrew's and most Linux distributions' Python refuse it.

You need a model served locally, and an agent:

Supported Tested end to end Model servers LM Studio, vLLM, Ollama, llama.cpp, mlx-lm LM Studio (macOS), vLLM (Linux) Agents opencode and pi (set up for you); any OpenAI-compatible tool opencode, pi Training Apple Silicon (MLX); NVIDIA and AMD (PyTorch) Apple Silicon, NVIDIA

Machines without a GPU still serve and record, but do not train. Tried Songe on another setup? Share the result on the testing board.

your agent ──► Songe (127.0.0.1:7613) ──► your model server │ records what happened ▼ when you are away: a Dream read lessons ─► practice ─► train ─► check ─► use only if better Quick Dream Deep Dream Takes a few minutes an hour or more Does adds the preferences you stated or showed to the model's instructions writes practice from your lessons and trains a small adapter on it You see each new preference, with a before/after where the answer changes why the new version was or was not used Undo undo the Quick Dream, or remove one preference go back to any earlier version

With auto-dream on, Dreams start when your agent has been quiet for a while. Or press Dream in the dashboard (songe open). A Dream never just disappears: it keeps going on the page, or says why it stopped.

How it learns, in more detail Reading. Songe reads each conversation for the moments that teach something: your corrections and stated rules, retries, tool errors. Practice. For each lesson your model writes short practice scenes in your agent's own tools. Your real conversations are never trained on. Training. The model as it was, shown the lesson, is the teacher; the same model with a small adapter, shown only the scene, is the student (on-policy distillation). Earlier skills are rehearsed so they stay. Checking. At the moments you reacted to, the version in use and the new one each answer, and a judge compares what they do. The new version is used only if it does clearly better, does not change what already worked, and its answers stay healthy.

Before the first training Songe measures how much your computer can learn at once, and trains on what fits. See DESIGN.md.

Command What it does songe what it is doing songe status --training [MODEL] resolved Deep Dream settings and where they come from songe open the dashboard in your browser songe models each model, and whether it dreams on its own songe models MODEL on|off auto-dream for one model songe sleep start a Deep Dream now songe undo MODEL go back one version songe pause / songe resume stop and restart learning songe doctor check the setup songe forget delete recorded conversations (learned versions stay) songe uninstall stop the service and restore your agent settings
What it changes on your machine Its data folder: ~/Library/Application Support/songe on macOS, $XDG_DATA_HOME/songe on Linux, %LOCALAPPDATA%\songe on Windows. A songe/ folder in LM Studio's models folder with the current learned version. Your own models are never touched. One provider entry in opencode and pi, with a backup. A background service that starts at login. Upgrade and remove

uv tool upgrade songe, pipx upgrade songe or brew upgrade songe: the service moves to the new version by itself in a quiet moment.

songe uninstall stops the service and restores your agent settings; add --purge to also delete its data and learned versions. Run it before brew uninstall songe.

Where Songe is going: ROADMAP.md. Ideas and bugs are welcome as issues. Questions and results from your nights go in Discord. To contribute, see CONTRIBUTING.md. Security reports: SECURITY.md.

entry.title: Jetty Pro
entry.content:
Hypercritical Jetty Pro

My first two Mac apps, Front and Center and SwitchGlass, were both created back in 2020 to restore features from DragThing, the venerable Mac app that was retired in 2019. The one tiny feature that Front and Center provided was literally a single checkbox within DragThing’s preferences. SwitchGlass went a bit farther, recreating one specific kind of floating palette from DragThing (and classic Mac OS).

After 24 years of development, DragThing had a ton of features. People often joked that I was destined to slowly reimplement all of DragThing’s functionality in a series of small apps. Put another way, they were saying I was doomed to make strange little Mac apps with extremely limited appeal (and sales).

Perhaps to prove them wrong, the next app I created was Hyperspace, which provided a way to reclaim disk space without removing any files. Hyperspace was still a nerdy app, but at least it had somewhat broader appeal than my earlier efforts. Who doesn’t want to save disk space? But more importantly, it was totally unrelated to DragThing. I had broken the curse!

Alas, there was one more (small) thing from DragThing that I missed. I used to have a DragThing palette in the corner of my screen containing some commonly used folders. In earlier versions of macOS, it was possible to pin the Dock to a screen corner, but that wasn’t really what I wanted either. I just wanted a small, separate palette of folders in the corner.

This is not a hard problem to solve. Plenty of Mac apps can provide something close to what I want…but not exactly what I want, in the specific way that I want it. For many years, I got by with some folders in the corner of my desktop. But the problem nagged at me.

A few years ago, I went so far as to implement my desired feature in SwitchGlass, adding the ability to create a small, extra palette full of folders in addition to the app switcher. But it felt incongruous with the rest of the app, so I never shipped it. And I didn’t want to maintain my own private fork of SwitchGlass, so I abandoned that branch of the code.

How It Started

Today, AI coding agents are helping to produce a bounty of new, niche Mac apps, many made by people who have little or no coding experience. Even for experienced software developers, vibe coding has made it possible to create apps that were previously “not worth building” due to an unfavorable ratio of effort to payoff.

It’s in this context that I revisited my “little palette of folders” idea. Surely I could vibe-code a simple app just for me in a day or two, right?

That was three and a half months ago.

How It’s Going

So what happened? The well-known programmer’s credo comes to mind: “We do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy.” Indeed.

I began the project by feeding a coding agent the source code to my app, SwitchGlass, as a starting point. I wrote SwitchGlass six years ago using a substantially more primitive version of SwiftUI. (For the developers out there, it predates @Observable and @State, and it supports Macs all the way back to macOS 12 Monterey from 2021.) I asked a coding agent to modernize the code and generalize it to support an arbitrary number of palettes instead of just one app switcher palette per display.

It worked, and quickly! But it was pretty shoddy. Many optimizations and niceties from SwitchGlass had been lost. So I dove in to fix them…and maybe add one or two more features, I guess…

Now, after months of work, I’ve created a bit of a monster. But in the process, I’ve fulfilled a long-held dream of mine—a dream I had set aside years ago because I thought it was impossible. I’ve replaced the Dock.

Only Apple…

If you’ve read any of my Mac OS X reviews, you know that I’ve always been dissatisfied with the Dock. Over the past couple of decades, I’ve gotten used to it, but I still bump up against its limitations and undesirable behaviors every day. (Undesirable to me, anyway.)

To pick just one example, I’ve always wanted clicking on a folder in the Dock to open that folder in the Finder. The Dock did work this way for several years, but in 2009’s Mac OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard (…I think?), Apple switched to requiring a Command-Option-click to open a folder in the Finder. Since then, I’ve been Command-Option-clicking folders in the Dock many, many times per day. It’s a small thing, but it adds up: seventeen years of Command-Option clicking!

But what could I do? I was forced to continue to use the Dock because there are so many things that “only the Dock can do” in macOS. I was reminded of this harsh reality when I created SwitchGlass. Why doesn’t SwitchGlass show notification badges? Why does the Calendar icon show today’s date in the Dock but not in SwitchGlass? Why don’t app icons in SwitchGlass bounce when the app needs attention? Why can’t I quit an app from SwitchGlass?

Though I did find a workaround for that last one, the answer to most of these questions is that third-party apps simply can’t do all the things the Dock can do. The Dock is part of the operating system, and it enjoys special privileges and deep integration that no third-party app can match.

This remains true today, especially for sandboxed apps sold through the Mac App Store like SwitchGlass (and all my other Mac apps). But what about apps that aren’t in the Mac App Store? What about unsandboxed apps? How close can they come to doing all the things the Dock does, especially if they use private APIs that are forbidden in the Mac App Store?

I aimed to find out. I hatched a plan, which I announced on episode 706 of Accidental Tech Podcast on August 26, 2026. I would create two apps: one called Jetty that would be sold through the Mac App Store, and a more powerful, unsandboxed app called Jetty Pro that would be distributed directly to customers, outside the Mac App Store.

But as I worked on the two apps, it became clear that “plain Jetty” was not that great. It had all the same limitations as SwitchGlass when it came to duplicating the features of the Dock. After less than two weeks of work, I abandoned plain Jetty and concentrated entirely on Jetty Pro.

After three and a half months of work, there are still things that only the Dock can do, but the list is not very long. I don’t expect most users to fully replace the Dock with Jetty Pro, but I’m happily doing so. If only my 2001 self could see me now!

Jetty Pro

Now, finally, I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. These palettes can contain any combination of files, folders, volumes, apps, Shortcuts, spacers, dividers, and even the Trash. If you’ve ever been unsatisfied with some aspect of how the Dock works, or if you’ve just wanted to augment the Dock with some additional palettes, try Jetty Pro and make your Mac’s interface work the way you want it to. Here are some of the highlights:

Jetty Pro palettes are extensively customizable. Nearly every palette layout metric can be adjusted. Jetty Pro can simulate the Dock backgrounds from macOS 15, 26, and 27, and it provides several of its own background appearances as well. The image at the top of this post shows just some of the possibilities.

Jetty Pro lets you customize the icon of any item in a palette—even the Finder. And if you’ve ever wanted to break an app out of Squircle Jail, now you can do it.

Unlike the macOS Dock, Jetty Pro will show folder label colors (without also setting a folder symbol). You can even apply color labels to folders independent of their labels in the Finder.

Don’t want to see “Running in Background” apps in macOS 27? Jetty Pro can hide them.

Want to hide notification badges for specific apps, but only in specific palettes? Jetty Pro can do that. And unlike the Dock, Jetty Pro can even hide notification badges on the System Settings app.

Jetty Pro can exclude or include running apps of your choice on a per-palette basis.

Jetty Pro lets you choose what happens when you click (or modifier-click) an app or folder in a palette.

A Jetty Pro palette can be configured to appear on a single display, selected displays, or on every display, while also choosing which attributes, like size and position, are allowed to vary per display.

Use Jetty Pro to augment the macOS Dock with additional palettes, or use it to replace the Dock entirely. It’s up to you.

Jetty Pro is available for a special introductory price of $9.99 per year (plus applicable taxes) until the end of 2026, with a 14-day free trial.

To learn more, including why a subscription is the only way to pay for Jetty Pro, please read the extensive documentation.

As you might have already guessed, Jetty Pro uses every private API it can get its hands on, and it requires a ton of special permissions, all of which are explained in the documentation. For sensible security reasons, macOS makes it (increasingly) cumbersome for users to grant these permissions. But Jetty Pro needs them to do what it does. Check Settings > General in Jetty Pro and make sure it says “All permissions have been granted” at the bottom. If not, click the “Details…” button for further instructions.

After a brief dalliance with more “mainstream” apps like Hyperspace, I’m back to making niche apps for Mac weirdos like me. To thine own self be true, I guess. I hope there are others out there who have longed to make the Dock work just slightly differently and are now able to do so thanks to Jetty Pro.

I’m sure many people reading this will think it’s ridiculous that I spent months battling the limitations of macOS to create what appears (to the undiscerning eye) to be a nearly identical clone of the Dock. What a waste of time! And what took so long anyway? This is a weekend project, at most!

First, I can assure you that the “simple” appearance of Jetty Pro belies the huge level of complexity and trickery required to do so many different things that macOS does not support and actively works against. If Jetty Pro really does seem simple in use, then I have done my job well. (And if you can see the seams, then that’s where I’ve failed to completely overcome a hostile system that doesn’t want to allow Jetty Pro to do what it needs to do.)

Second, I put a tremendous amount of time and effort into Jetty Pro. The documentation alone (which, like every word in every post on this website, was written by me and me alone) took weeks to create. During the lead up to Jetty Pro 1.0, I’ve released over 160 builds to my 250 beta testers—more than one build per day. The Jetty Pro app icon was created by the fine humans at The Iconfactory. From the start, I’ve treated Jetty Pro like a “real” app, not a throwaway vibe-coded project.

Having spent so many years with the Dock as a tiny pebble in my shoe, the difference between it and Jetty Pro means everything to me. Like Front and Center and SwitchGlass before it, I’m now running Jetty Pro all day, every day on my Mac. Replacing the Dock with Jetty Pro has made me happier than any other app I’ve created. I hope it will make some other Mac weirdos happy too.

entry.title: Active intrusion campaign against Check Point security management servers
entry.content:
GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.

Campaign Summary GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally. We are tracking this set of threat activity as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) which represents adversary infrastructure, tools and post-exploitation action against the 22 victims. The campaign targeting does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector. The impacted orgs include victims with assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the United States. The victim orgs sit in sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing. We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin. The actor used 99 IP addresses, much of which were disposable network infrastructure to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control of its victims, including the use of a compromised server acting as an “operational relay box” (ORB) or more simply, a “hop,” for interacting with downstream victim assets. The actor used this relay box / hop to save command results and data stolen from 24 distinct Check Point Security Management Servers. The actor used Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. The threat actor used or attempted to exploit multiple CVEs, including, but not limited to: CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF). Though we observed hands-on-keyboard activity, we believe that like most modern attacks, the actor used LLMs and agentic systems to perform vulnerability scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction with compromised assets. Our visibility into this attack activity stopped around November 2nd, 2026, but given the actor’s persistent access to victim Check Point devices, we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing. We are working with international government partners and CERTs to share relevant intelligence and notify the victims. Observed Attacker Activities

We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

HFS Scanning and Exploitation

The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500.

2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password.

Example POST to loginSrp1 and response

Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested

2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server.

Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie

Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits.

2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.

On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.

Establishing the Operational Relay Box / Hop

2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.

Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.

Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.

The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.

Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant

They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.

2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.

The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.

Intrusion Operations and Exfiltration

Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.

Between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.

The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.

2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server.

Excerpt from exploit.py - This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers.

2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment.

Excerpt from spray_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim.

2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and launched pull_<redacted_id>.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server.

Excerpt from pull_<redacted_id>.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration.

2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance.

2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04 UTC - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment.

CVE-2020-1472 (Microsoft Netlogon), CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Netscaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti Connect Secure), CVE-2021-26855/34473 (Microsoft Exchange) and CVE-2021-21972 / CVE-2023-34048 (VMware vCenter)

2026-10-21 11:41:21 UTC - The actor uses comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py to scan a variety of targets in Victim A’s network. Note that these scripts contain usernames and passwords that were themed to the target victim. The actor either knew or was guessing names and passwords that the target might use.

Excerpt from comb.py

Excerpt from ssh_comb.py

Excerpt from ssh_spray.py

2026-10-26 02:17:30 UTC - The actor issued a bulk certificate managing task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. The results of this task were shipped back to the hop server in a text file. We did not observe the actor sending this command task to these devices, indicating that it was issued from another part of the adversary’s infrastructure.

Note that these text files contained the victim IP addresses and were in incrementing IP order, indicating an automation looped through them to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers, and deliver them via scp to this exfil folder. Each file was delivered from victim infrastructure, showing that each of the compromised devices hold the SSH private key that matches the public key planted on the hop.

All of these files contain error messages which indicate that the certificate task failed. Though we did not see follow-on attempts, the task information and IP addresses from these outputs were enough for us to identify and notify many of the victim organizations either directly or through government partners.

Excerpt from sample /root/exfil/pc_XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.txt

One of the error messages had a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant on the device.

After the certificate minting failures, the actor’s activity dropped again until November 2nd.

Protecting Their Access

2026-11-02 02:28:27 UTC - By early November, other threat actors had begun to scan and attempt to abuse the compromised server. We observed the GT13 actor use a script to perform a self-check for a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug (CVE-2026-98432). After the check, the actor attempted to patch the system using Linux’s own command-line tool nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that may trigger the bug. This allowed the actor to protect their hop from others engaging in future exploitation of the bug.

Excerpt from cve_2026_98432.py

Example commands of the actor testing a CVE-2026-98432 script on the hop box, and then attempting to patch the vulnerability with nftables, the built-in Linux firewall and packet-filtering framework. You’ll notice the patching commands happened quickly.

Notes on Attack Timeframe and Timeline The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server. We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets. We observed GT13 attack activity between 2026-10-02 13:17:45 and 2026-11-02 03:19:46 UTC. During our observation of the actor, we did not observe any adversary hands-on-keyboard activity between ~17:00 UTC and ~00:19 UTC, and nothing in the 05:00 UTC hour. We know the risks of time zone analysis and do not put much weight into the actor’s tendency to operate in what would be a convenient UTC+7- or UTC+8 workday. The attack infrastructure was long established before we first saw it, as we note the attempted malware domain newpayapp[.]com was first registered on 2026-03-13 12:46:28 UTC. It may be a UTC+7-friendly coincidence that the domain was originally created with the registrant state as “Hai Phong” with country code “VN” (see Cloudflare’s RDAP service). We suspect the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus. We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets. We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations.

entry.title: From CUDA and Jax to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver
entry.content:
From CUDA and JAX to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver

Some time ago, I shared a blog post about working with Cayley graphs, where I solved combinatorial puzzles using AI coding agents, PyTorch on GPUs, and JAX on TPUs. Recently, Google released TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for TPUs, and I wanted to see how well it works on the same task: whether a PyTorch-native TPU stack could match my A100 training pipeline and my JAX beam search in speed and solution quality, or maybe even beat them.

The short version: getting TorchTPU to work was easy; getting it to work efficiently was considerably harder. My initial training port was 1.65x slower than the A100 implementation, while the first TPU beam search was 5.7x slower than its JAX counterpart.

After optimizing eager execution, rewriting attention, eliminating dynamic tensor shapes, fixing a subtle deduplication bug, and investigating an attention-routing regression, the results changed substantially. Training reached comparable wall-clock performance to the A100, and the optimized TorchTPU beam search became 25% faster per level than JAX on the same eight-chip v6e machine, producing the same total solution length across six test puzzles.

Along the way, the investigation improved the solver itself and resulted in an upstream TorchTPU GitHub issue that led to attention-routing fixes.

The code is available on Kaggle notebooks running on a free TPU v5e-8:

As in the previous post, the code and the experiments were done by coding agents (Claude Code and Codex): I decided what to port, what to measure, and how to judge the results, and they did the implementation and the profiling.

The problem

The CayleyPy Professor Tetraminx competition requires finding the shortest sequence of moves that solves 1000 scrambled puzzles. Formally, it is a shortest-path problem in a Cayley graph (each puzzle state is a node, and each of the 24 possible moves is an edge) with an 88-sticker state.

My solver uses beam search guided by a learned neural heuristic — a 3.4M-parameter PieceTransformer. Instead of treating the 88 stickers individually, it groups them into 50 physical pieces, turns each piece into a token, adds a class token (51 tokens in total), and runs four small transformer layers with eight heads of size 32. At the end, an all-neighbours Q head (a head that predicts, for each of the 24 moves, the distance to solved after that move) outputs 24 numbers. So the beam scores all 24 children of a state with one forward pass on the parent.

For training, the signal is a mix of cheap random walks and exact ground truth:

Random walks of 2–40 moves from the solved state. A state p moves into a walk has two known labels: undoing the last move gives distance p - 1, and continuing the walk gives p + 1.Exact 24-way labels from a breadth-first search (BFS) table at depth 5 or less.The puzzle’s 24 spatial symmetries, used as data augmentation.

On the A100, one epoch takes 142.7 seconds. My best checkpoint is epoch 1500 of a 2000-epoch run, about 80 hours in total.

What is TorchTPU

TorchTPU is not PyTorch/XLA: there is no LazyTensor tracing, no xm.mark_step(), and no xla_device(). Instead, TorchTPU lowers ATen ops directly to StableHLO and runs through PJRT and libtpu (PyTorch’s core ops are translated straight into XLA’s input format and executed by the TPU runtime). Once you import torch, "tpu" works as a device string just like "cuda".

It has three execution modes:

Eager (the default): runs one op at a time asynchronously.Fused eager (TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1): defers ops and fuses them across op boundaries without needing torch.compile.Compiled (torch.compile(fn, dynamic=False)): graph compilation targeting the TPU backend.

Three rules matter in practice:

Static shapes were the reliable path: with the TorchTPU builds and operators I used, fixed tensor shapes and torch.compile(..., dynamic=False) worked best, and every new shape meant a full recompile.Data-dependent output sizes were the most expensive: ops like nonzero, masked_select, unique, bincount, and even x[bool_mask] still run in eager mode, but they force a .cpu().item() host round-trip to learn their output size, and a compiled graph gets specialized to that one size, so each new size means another compile.Nothing falls back silently to the CPU: an op that TorchTPU doesn’t implement raises an error instead of quietly running slowly.Part 1: training, from 1.65x slower to 1.08x faster

I ran the first port on a Cloud TPU machine with four v6e chips, using DDP with one process per chip and a global batch of 512, so each epoch saw exactly the same number of samples as on the A100. Before the code could run on the TPU at all, I had to remove four GPU idioms (masked_select in the loss, boolean-mask indexing when expanding labels, 12 .item() metric reads per step, and sampling training anchors on the CPU instead of keeping the 0.19 GB anchor table in TPU memory). This first working version took 234.8 seconds per epoch, 1.65x slower than the A100. I was able to bring it down to 132 seconds with two changes.

Fused eager

The first win was practically free: turning on fused eager (TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1). Only the model’s forward and backward pass ran under torch.compile; the rest of the trainer (the random-walk sampler with its 40-iteration loop, label expansion, the loss, and the metrics) ran in eager mode, one op at a time. In default eager mode, that data pipeline took 61.3 ms per step. Wrapping it in torch.compile brought it down to 29.7 ms, while fused eager, which fuses the ops at run time without any code changes, got it to 13.1 ms. The pipeline is many tiny ops, and on this workload they fused better than they compiled; I didn’t profile why, since the cheaper option was also the faster one. Setting that single environment variable dropped the epoch time from 234.8 s to 176.5 s.

The attention rewrite that was almost thrown away

Still, 176.5 s was slower than the A100, and the GPU profile didn’t help. On the A100, the input stage and embedding gradient took 67% of the step; on the TPU, the same stage took only 0.96 ms (0.8%), and the model was spending ~90% of its time in attention.

A roofline at the model’s own shapes explained why. A square 8192³ GEMM hits 361 TFLOP/s on one v6e chip, and the model’s QKV and FFN GEMMs hit 212–259 TFLOP/s, while attention ran at 3.0 TFLOP/s. With T = 51 and head_dim = 32, every attention matmul is 51x32x51 on a 128x128 matrix unit (MXU) — roughly 2.5% tile occupancy. Padding head_dim to 128 or T to 64 actually made things slower (0.83x and 0.81x). As a result, attention is about 3% of the model’s FLOPs but about 90% of its time on the TPU.

If you want to keep the same model (for a fair comparison), you need to keep the same shapes and find other improvements. Standard scaled_dot_product_attention (SDPA) expects (B, H, T, Dh), so the QKV tensor has to be permuted to move the heads to the second dimension. Rewriting attention with torch.einsum keeps the heads in their original dimension and avoids the permutes:

q, k, v = qkv.view(B, T, 3, H, Dh).unbind(2) # heads never leave dim 2 s = torch.einsum("bthd,bshd->bhts", q, k) * scale p = s.float().softmax(-1).to(v.dtype) # fp32 softmax, on purpose a = torch.einsum("bhts,bshd->bthd", p, v)

The fp32 softmax is there for numerics. On the TPU, the einsum and SDPA versions disagreed by a relative 3.3e-3, so I checked both against a float64 reference on the CPU: both were about 4.6e-3 away from it, because the TPU’s matrix unit uses a single-pass bf16 multiply even for “fp32” matmuls unless you raise torch.tpu.precision. In bf16, keeping only the softmax in fp32 closed the remaining gap between the two versions.

This change was almost rejected. The agent first measured it on the forward pass only, where it looked slower (einsum 5.51 ms vs SDPA 4.56 ms), and discarded it on that basis. Thankfully, I decided to check the full forward+backward pass: the profiler attributed much of the backward-pass overhead to layout conversions around SDPA’s saved tensors, which cost far more than the forward pass saved. Across forward+backward, one layer dropped from 25.14 ms to 14.85 ms (1.69x faster). That pushed the whole epoch down to 132.0 s — 1.08x faster than the A100.

A checkpoint with deadlocks

The most confusing bug was in checkpointing. Saving a checkpoint only from rank 0 is a standard pattern:

if is_main: torch.save(model.state_dict(), path) # deadlocks under fused eager + DDP

Under fused eager, the tensors in state_dict are still deferred. When rank 0 reads them, it executes a graph that includes this step’s DDP collectives, while the other ranks are already waiting at the next barrier. The checkpoint file would grow to 1.1 MB, then 2.2 MB, and freeze forever while every rank sat busy. The fix is to move the tensors to the CPU on every rank and write the file on one:

cpu_state = {k: v.detach().to("cpu") for k, v in model.state_dict().items()} # all ranks if is_main: torch.save(cpu_state, path)

The trap only fires in the mode that gives the speedup, which made it harder to find.

Summary of training changesWhat changedWhy it mattered on TPUImpactmasked_select / x[bool_mask] → where / scatter_Avoids data-dependent output sizes, host syncs, and recompilesRequired for static graphs12 .item() reads → device accumulator; host anchors → HBMEliminates per-step graph cuts and cpu transfers (0.19 GB table)Clean async executionTORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1Fuses tiny eager ops in the sampler, loss, and metrics1.33x faster epochattn_impl="einsum" (training only)Avoids layout conversions around SDPA’s saved tensors in the backward pass1.34x faster epochMaterialize state_dict on all ranksPrevents deferred DDP collectives from deadlocking rank 0Fixes checkpoint hangSame validation size in smoke test and full runAvoids a 28736-row validation graph OOM at epoch 25Unblocked the Kaggle full run
